cards.text: When a horse is favourite for a big race, people who have bet against it, or who stand to lose if it wins, have a reason to stop it running.
cards.exceptions: The owner or backers of the favourite normally want it to run.

cards.text: A famous racehorse is large, valuable and recognisable, and it is hard to hide or move unseen in open, thinly settled country.
cards.exceptions: It can be hidden if it is disguised, kept in a building, or killed.

cards.text: In detective stories, what the detective asks for, looks at, or finds odd usually matters later.
Readers of the period readily suspected roaming gypsies of horse-stealing.
cards.exceptions: It is a prejudice of the time, not evidence, and a large reward puts the same people on the side of finding the horse.

cards.text: A drug mixed into food is easier to give unnoticed in a strongly flavoured dish than in a plain one, because most drugs have a taste or smell of their own.
cards.exceptions: Tasteless drugs; a very small dose; a careless or very hungry eater.

cards.text: The master of a stable or house normally keeps a key to it.
cards.exceptions: Keys may be held only by the servant on duty, or kept at a separate office.

cards.text: A guard dog kept in a building gives the alarm when strangers come at night.
cards.exceptions: It is drugged, removed, or out of earshot, or it knows the visitor.

cards.text: A man struck hard on the head can thrash about convulsively and may hurt himself with anything he is holding.
Something lost out of doors can be picked up and carried off by anyone who comes across it, so where it turns up later does not prove where its owner went.
cards.exceptions: It was lost only moments before, or in a place nobody else could reach.

cards.text: Searchers look for what they have been told to look for, so a search finds a thing only if it still looks the way it was described.
cards.exceptions: Searchers who know the object closely, or who check it in ways that do not depend on appearance.

cards.text: Racing touts commonly paid stable-lads money for inside information on how the horses were running.
A cataract knife is an eye-surgeon's instrument: a very thin, rigid, extremely sharp blade made for tiny, precise cuts, not for fighting.
When a man has letters for a 'friend' sent to his own house, the friend may be the man himself under another name.
cards.exceptions: A genuine friend who has no fixed address, or who has a real reason to receive post elsewhere.

cards.text: A man secretly paying for costly women's clothes, under a name not his own, is often keeping a woman his wife does not know about, and such a life needs more money than his wages.
cards.exceptions: Gifts to a relative; a debt he is settling for someone else.

cards.text: Someone who carries a candle and matches at night means to need a small light somewhere, usually out of the wind and away from other lamps.
cards.exceptions: He carries them by habit, or to light a pipe.

cards.text: A detective may make a false remark on purpose so that the answer reveals something the person would not volunteer.
On a still night a garment does not end up on a bush by itself. If it is found draped there, someone put it there.
cards.exceptions: It was caught and dragged during a struggle, or thrown and snagged by chance.

cards.text: A man takes off a heavy coat in bad weather when he needs his arms free for close work or for exertion.
cards.exceptions: It is torn off him, or he is too hot from running.

cards.text: A shod horse moving over soft, wet ground leaves hoof-prints that a careful searcher can follow, and a cast shoe can be matched against them.
cards.exceptions: Hard or stony ground, heavy trampling, or ground searched too narrowly.

cards.text: An owner withdraws a horse from a race when he believes it cannot run. Someone who advises keeping the entry expects the horse to be back and fit in time.
cards.exceptions: Keeping the entry as a bluff, or to avoid losing a forfeit.

cards.text: A horse is a herd animal. Left loose, it tends to make for its own stable or for other horses nearby rather than roam alone.
cards.exceptions: It is badly frightened, injured, shut in, or caught by someone.

cards.text: A horse's distinctive markings, such as a white blaze, can be dyed or painted over so that it passes for another horse, and later washed back.
cards.exceptions: Searchers who know the horse closely by build, gait or temperament.

cards.text: A detective who asks for someone's photograph usually means to show it to a witness who may recognise that person, perhaps under another name.
Someone who must perform a delicate operation he has never done before tends to practise it first on something less valuable.
cards.exceptions: A practised hand; no time or opportunity to rehearse.

cards.text: A small cut to a horse's leg tendon can make it go slightly lame, so that it runs badly without any obvious wound.
A horse that is hurt or frightened at close quarters can kick with enough force to kill a man.
When a horse's price shortens sharply just before a race, with nothing announced, it usually means that people with inside knowledge are backing it heavily.
cards.exceptions: A rumour that turns out false; general public enthusiasm; a bookmaker cutting his exposure.

thoughts.reads: the singular disappearance of the favourite for the Wessex Cup, and the tragic murder of its trainer
thoughts.text: Two events: the favourite for the Wessex Cup has vanished, and its trainer has been murdered.
How are the disappearance and the murder connected?
options: A thief came for the horse and killed the trainer who got in the way
The two are separate, or only linked by coincidence
The trainer was mixed up in what happened to the horse

thoughts.text: What does 'disappearance' mean for the horse?
options: Stolen and hidden
Strayed loose in the confusion
Killed or maimed and the body not yet found

thoughts.text: Who gains if the favourite does not run? Bookmakers, people who bet against it, rival owners. Who would want the trainer dead?
options: Someone with money riding against the favourite
A rival stable
Someone with a private grudge against the trainer

thoughts.reads: You would oblige me by bringing with you your very excellent field-glass.
thoughts.text: Holmes wants a field-glass before he has seen the ground. He expects to look at something at a distance: open moor, a racecourse, figures far off. Keep it in mind.

thoughts.reads: there are points about the case which promise to make it an absolutely unique one
thoughts.text: Holmes already sees particular 'points', apparently from the newspaper reports alone. The clues may be in the facts he is about to list.

thoughts.reads: Our rate at present is fifty-three and a half miles an hour.
thoughts.text: The speed calculation from the telegraph posts shows off Holmes's method. It has no bearing on the case.

thoughts.reads: this matter of the murder of John Straker and the disappearance of Silver Blaze
thoughts.text: Names: the trainer is John Straker, and the horse is Silver Blaze.

thoughts.reads: the art of the reasoner should be used rather for the sifting of details than for the acquiring of fresh evidence
thoughts.text: Holmes says the answer lies in the facts already known, once they are cleared of journalists' theorising. So the reader should treat his coming summary as the evidence to sift, and distrust press 'conjecture'.

thoughts.reads: I received telegrams from both Colonel Ross, the owner of the horse, and from Inspector Gregory, who is looking after the case, inviting my co-operation
thoughts.text: Colonel Ross owns the horse, and Inspector Gregory leads the police case. Both called Holmes in on Tuesday evening.

thoughts.reads: And this is Thursday morning.
thoughts.text: The telegrams came Tuesday evening, so the crime happened no later than Tuesday, probably Monday night or Tuesday. Two days have now passed.

thoughts.reads: I could not believe it possible that the most remarkable horse in England could long remain concealed, especially in so sparsely inhabited a place as the north of Dartmoor
thoughts.text: Holmes reasoned as anyone would: a famous horse on an empty moor gets found quickly.
The horse cannot have simply strayed. A loose favourite on a thinly peopled moor would have turned up within two days. Someone is keeping it out of sight, or it is dead.
How can so conspicuous a horse stay unfound? Turn it around: what would make the usual rule fail here?
options: Shut in a building nearby
Changed in appearance so that nobody recognises it
Taken a long way off very quickly
Dead, and the body hidden

thoughts.reads: I expected to hear that he had been found, and that his abductor was the murderer of John Straker
thoughts.text: Working theory, Holmes's own until now: one person took the horse and killed Straker.

thoughts.reads: beyond the arrest of young Fitzroy Simpson nothing had been done
thoughts.text: The police have arrested a young man, Fitzroy Simpson.
Simpson is the abductor and murderer.
options: Simpson did both
Simpson did one or the other
Simpson is innocent and was arrested on suspicion

thoughts.text: Holmes treats the arrest as 'nothing having been done'. To him an arrest does not settle the case, especially with the horse still missing. If Simpson knew where the horse was, one might expect it to have been found by now.

thoughts.reads: Yet in some ways I feel that yesterday has not been wasted.
thoughts.text: The fact that the horse was not found is itself information to Holmes. Its continued absence is a clue to how it is being hidden.

Open at the end of the scene: how the murder and the disappearance connect; where an unfindable famous horse can be; who profits if the favourite does not run; whether Simpson is more than a convenient arrest; and what Holmes means to look at with the field-glass. The details have not been given yet. Holmes's list of facts comes next and should be read closely.

Leading picture so far: someone with an interest against the favourite stole or harmed Silver Blaze, killed Straker in the process, and has hidden the horse well. Simpson is the police's candidate. It is held loosely, because Holmes's own version of it has already failed once.

thoughts.reads: the betting being three to one on him
thoughts.text: Silver Blaze is heavily odds-on for the Wessex Cup.

thoughts.reads: preventing Silver Blaze from being there at the fall of the flag next Tuesday
thoughts.text: The race is next Tuesday, about five days off. Whoever has the horse needs to keep it out of sight only until then.

thoughts.reads: so that even at those odds enormous sums of money have been laid upon him
thoughts.text: Huge sums are bet on him, so the bookmakers who took those bets stand to lose heavily if he wins. Layers against the favourite are the obvious class of suspect.

thoughts.reads: has always shown himself to be a zealous and honest servant
thoughts.text: Straker is a former jockey with twelve years' good service to the Colonel. His character is reported as excellent.

thoughts.reads: One of these lads sat up each night in the stable, while the others slept in the loft
thoughts.text: Routine: one lad sits up in the stable each night and the other two sleep in the loft above.

thoughts.reads: lived in a small villa about two hundred yards from the stables
thoughts.text: Map: Straker's house is 200 yards from the stables and a cluster of villas lies half a mile north. Tavistock is two miles west, and Mapleton is two miles across the moor. Everything else is empty moor.

thoughts.reads: the larger training establishment of Mapleton, which belongs to Lord Backwater, and is managed by Silas Brown
thoughts.text: A rival training stable two miles off is one place where a horse could stand unnoticed among other horses, under cover. It answers the 'shut in a building' option of t14.3.
options: Mapleton is hiding the horse
Mapleton is mere geography

thoughts.reads: inhabited only by a few roaming gypsies
thoughts.text: A reader of the time would think at once of the gypsies as horse-thieves. That is a candidate the story itself puts on the map.

thoughts.reads: the stables were locked up at nine o’clock
thoughts.text: The stables were locked at nine. Ned Hunter stayed inside on guard, and the other two lads went up to the house for supper.

thoughts.reads: which consisted of a dish of curried mutton
thoughts.text: Edith Baxter, the maid, carried Hunter's supper down to the stables. It was curried mutton.

thoughts.reads: it was the rule that the lad on duty should drink nothing else
thoughts.text: The duty lad drinks only tap water. So if anyone wanted to dose him, the food is the only channel. The menu is told in unusual detail.

thoughts.reads: carried a heavy stick with a knob to it
thoughts.text: The stranger is gentlemanly, wears a grey tweed suit and cloth cap with gaiters, and carries a heavy knobbed stick. He is pale and nervous, and a little over thirty.

thoughts.reads: I understand that a stable-boy sleeps there alone every night.
thoughts.text: He claimed to be lost (¶22), yet he knows the stable routine. The 'lost' story is a pretext, and he came to this stable on purpose.

thoughts.reads: He took a piece of white paper folded up out of his waistcoat pocket.
thoughts.text: What is in the folded paper?
options: A drug for the boy's supper
A note or bribe-offer for the boy
Money

thoughts.reads: It was already opened, and Hunter was seated at the small table inside.
thoughts.text: Meals are handed in through a window that was already open, with Hunter at a table just inside.

thoughts.reads: The girl has sworn that as he spoke she noticed the corner of the little paper packet protruding from his closed hand.
thoughts.text: This is sworn, but it comes from a frightened girl by lantern light, and it fits what everyone later came to believe. It shows the packet was still in his hand. It does not show what was done with it.

thoughts.reads: You’ve two horses in for the Wessex Cup—Silver Blaze and Bayard.
thoughts.text: King's Pyland has two runners. The stranger asks whether the stable secretly prefers Bayard. That is a tout's question.

thoughts.reads: rushed across the stable to unloose the dog
thoughts.text: There is a guard dog kept in the stable.

thoughts.reads: as she ran she looked back and saw that the stranger was leaning through the window
thoughts.text: While Hunter crossed the stable for the dog, the stranger was alone at the open window with the supper on the table inside. He had the chance to put something in it.

thoughts.reads: Did the stable-boy, when he ran out with the dog, leave the door unlocked behind him?
thoughts.text: Watson's idea: the stranger doubled back and slipped in, or someone else did, while Hunter was out with the dog and the door stood open.

thoughts.reads: The boy locked the door before he left it.
thoughts.text: The door was locked and the window is too small for a man to get through. The stranger did not get in that evening.
Holmes wired specially about the door. Access to the stable is a key point for him: whoever took the horse later had to get through a locked door.

thoughts.reads: he pulled on his large mackintosh and left the house
thoughts.text: Straker went out at about 1 a.m. in the rain to check the stables, wearing a large mackintosh.

thoughts.reads: although he does not seem to have quite realized its true significance
thoughts.text: He is said not to have grasped the significance, yet he was uneasy enough to go out alone at one in the rain without waking the lads. Mrs Straker reports only the reason he gave her.

thoughts.reads: Hunter was sunk in a state of absolute stupor
thoughts.text: At 7 a.m.: the stable door is open, Hunter is stupefied, the stall is empty and Straker is missing.

thoughts.reads: The door was open
thoughts.text: Locked at nine and open at seven: who opened it?
options: Someone with a duplicate or stolen key
Straker, who would have a key as master of the stable
Hunter, before the drug took hold

thoughts.reads: They had heard nothing during the night, for they are both sound sleepers.
thoughts.text: The lads in the loft heard nothing.
A guard dog is kept in the stable, yet nothing woke the lads overhead. Did the dog make no noise while the horse was taken? The account does not say.
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must connect the dog of ¶29 with the silence of ¶34. They are five paragraphs apart and the dog is never mentioned again.

thoughts.reads: John Straker’s overcoat was flapping from a furze-bush
thoughts.text: Straker's coat was hanging on a furze-bush a quarter-mile from the stables. His body lay in a hollow just beyond.
It was a rainy night, yet his coat is off and hung on a bush. Why would he take it off?
options: It was torn off in the struggle
He threw it aside to fight
He took it off for some task
Someone else put it there

thoughts.reads: there was a long, clean cut, inflicted evidently by some very sharp instrument
thoughts.text: Wounds: his head was smashed by a heavy weapon, and he has a long clean cut on the thigh from a very sharp blade.

thoughts.reads: in his right hand he held a small knife, which was clotted with blood up to the handle
thoughts.text: Straker held a small, bloodied knife in his right hand.
Straker went out to check on horses carrying a knife. What kind of knife, and why did he have it? It is described only as 'small'.

thoughts.reads: in his left he clasped a red and black silk cravat
thoughts.text: In his left hand was a cravat that the maid identifies as the stranger's.

thoughts.reads: He was equally certain that the same stranger had, while standing at the window, drugged his curried mutton
thoughts.text: Hunter did not see the drugging. He concluded it. He was across the stable fetching the dog. It is a reasonable guess, but it is not observation.

thoughts.reads: there were abundant proofs in the mud which lay at the bottom of the fatal hollow that he had been there at the time of the struggle
thoughts.text: The horse was in the hollow where Straker died, at the time of the struggle.

thoughts.reads: all the gypsies of Dartmoor are on the alert
thoughts.text: With a large reward and the gypsies themselves searching, a gypsy theft looks less likely. So does a horse that is merely loose. The horse is hidden well, or in a place nobody searches.

thoughts.reads: contain an appreciable quantity of powdered opium
thoughts.text: Hunter's leftover curry contains powdered opium.

thoughts.reads: the people at the house partook of the same dish on the same night without any ill effect
thoughts.text: The household ate the same dish unharmed, so the opium went into Hunter's portion only. It was added after his share was set apart: in the kitchen, on the path, at the window, or by Hunter himself.
The analysis confirms that Hunter really was drugged. That makes him an unlikely accomplice who opened the door.

Powdered opium has a taste of its own, and a curry would hide it. A stranger who met the maid by chance on the path could not have known the supper would be curry. Would a plain dish have given the drug away?
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader needs to know that opium has a noticeable taste, and to ask whether the poisoner chose the dish or was merely lucky. Few readers make this step unprompted.

thoughts.reads: Were he but gifted with imagination he might rise to great heights in his profession.
thoughts.text: Holmes calls Gregory competent but unimaginative. The 'natural' suspect the police chose may be the wrong one.

thoughts.reads: he inhabited one of those villas which I have mentioned
thoughts.text: Simpson was lodging in the villas half a mile north and was found there easily.

thoughts.reads: bets to the amount of five thousand pounds had been registered by him against the favourite
thoughts.text: Simpson is a ruined gentleman who now makes a book, and he stands to lose £5,000 if Silver Blaze wins. He has a strong motive.

thoughts.reads: He did not attempt to deny that he had acted as described upon the evening before
thoughts.text: The stranger at the window is Simpson. He admits it.

thoughts.reads: Desborough, the second favourite, which was in charge of Silas Brown at the Mapleton stables
thoughts.text: Mapleton, two miles off and run by Silas Brown, has Desborough, the second favourite.
Mapleton gains directly if Silver Blaze is out of the race. Silas Brown has both motive and a nearby stable to hide a horse in.
options: Mapleton people took the horse
Mapleton is only a rival, not involved

thoughts.reads: he turned very pale, and was utterly unable to account for its presence in the hand of the murdered man
thoughts.text: Simpson does not deny the cravat is his. Turning pale fits guilt, and it also fits a man who sees he is in serious trouble. He did not deny being at the stable either, so where did he lose the cravat?

thoughts.reads: his stick, which was a Penang-lawyer weighted with lead
thoughts.text: Simpson's clothes were wet from the night's storm. His knobbed stick is lead-weighted and could have caused the head wound.

thoughts.reads: there was no wound upon his person
thoughts.text: Simpson is unwounded, though Straker's knife is bloody to the handle. Whose blood is on it? Either another assailant is wounded, or the blood came from somewhere else.

thoughts.reads: one at least of his assailants must bear his mark upon him
thoughts.text: The account speaks of 'assailants', plural. It is unclear whether that is evidence or reporters' framing. Nothing shown so far requires more than one.

thoughts.reads: the incised wound upon Straker may have been caused by his own knife in the convulsive struggles which follow any brain injury
thoughts.text: Watson's idea: Straker cut his own thigh in convulsions after the blow. The blood on the knife would then be his own.

thoughts.reads: It is more than possible; it is probable
thoughts.text: If the cut is self-inflicted, Simpson's lack of a wound proves nothing, and the case against him gets stronger.

thoughts.reads: His bridle is missing, so that Simpson must have put this on.
thoughts.text: The horse's bridle is missing. Someone led him out bridled.

thoughts.reads: having in some way obtained a duplicate key
thoughts.text: Police theory: Simpson drugged Hunter, used a duplicate key, bridled and led off the horse, met Straker, killed him with the stick, and then either hid the horse or lost it when it bolted.

thoughts.reads: I am afraid that whatever theory we state has very grave objections to it
thoughts.text: The police theory leaves gaps. Where did Simpson get a duplicate key? Why would a man betting against the horse lead it away rather than just harm it in the stall? Where is it now, with Simpson under arrest? The 'bolted' branch conflicts with t14.2, since a loose horse would have been found. It does not explain Straker's coat on the bush, or why Simpson stayed at his lodging to be arrested.

Another reading of the same facts: Straker himself opened the stable and took the horse out. He had a key, went out alone at one, died beside the horse, had his coat off and a knife in hand. If so, why, and who killed him?
options: Straker took the horse out for an innocent reason and met the thief
Straker was himself acting against the horse
Straker followed someone who had taken it
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must set aside Straker's reported good character and the account's framing of him as victim. They must then join the locked door, his key and his solitary night walk.

thoughts.text: Open at the scene's end: who opened the locked door, and where the horse is hidden. Whether the stranger really drugged the curry or Hunter only assumed it, and how a passer-by could rely on a dish that hides opium. Why the coat was off, what the knife was for, and whether the dog was silent. What part Mapleton and Silas Brown play. What Holmes wants the field-glass for. Simpson remains the police's suspect, and the theory is admitted to be improbable.

thoughts.reads: The latter was Colonel Ross, the well-known sportsman; the other, Inspector Gregory
thoughts.text: Ross and Gregory meet Holmes and Watson at Tavistock station. Gregory is the tall, fair man and Ross is the small, dapper one with an eye-glass.

thoughts.reads: I wish to leave no stone unturned in trying to avenge poor Straker and in recovering my horse
thoughts.text: Ross wants Straker avenged and the horse recovered. As owner of the favourite, he is someone who wants it to run.

thoughts.reads: I am sorry to say that we have made very little progress
thoughts.text: Nothing new since Holmes's summary. The horse is still missing.

thoughts.reads: Colonel Ross leaned back with his arms folded and his hat tilted over his eyes
thoughts.text: The owner takes no part in the talk about his own horse. He may doubt the detectives, or he may simply be a cold man. It is probably manner rather than clue.

thoughts.reads: I recognise that the evidence is purely circumstantial
thoughts.text: Gregory is sure Simpson is the man, and he admits the case is circumstantial. His theory matches the one Holmes predicted (t46.2).

thoughts.reads: We have quite come to the conclusion that he wounded himself in his fall.
thoughts.text: The police independently reached Watson's idea that the cut on Straker's thigh came from his own knife.

thoughts.reads: He lies under suspicion of having poisoned the stable-boy
thoughts.text: Even Gregory puts this only as 'suspicion'. It rests on Hunter's conclusion, not on anyone seeing it done: the maid saw a packet in his hand and then saw him lean through the window.

thoughts.reads: Why should he take the horse out of the stable? If he wished to injure it why could he not do it there?
thoughts.text: Holmes's objection, turned around: who would need the horse out on the open moor rather than in the stall? Someone who had to do something to it that could not be done inside, or someone who meant to take it away.
options: A thief meaning to hide or sell it
Someone who needed it out of the stable for a reason not yet known
Someone leading it to a confederate

thoughts.reads: What chemist sold him the powdered opium?
thoughts.text: Holmes asks where the opium came from. He treats it as something that can be traced. The opium links to the curry question (t37.6).

thoughts.reads: What is his own explanation as to the paper which he wished the maid to give to the stable-boy?
thoughts.text: The folded paper is still unexplained. Holmes wants Simpson's account of it.

thoughts.reads: He says that it was a ten-pound note. One was found in his purse.
thoughts.text: Simpson says the paper was a ten-pound note, and one was found in his purse.

A ten-pound note is exactly what a tout would offer a lad for a tip, and the note was still in his purse. That fits 'bribe for information' better than 'drug'. If the packet was money, the only evidence that he drugged the curry gets weaker. Hunter's belief in t36.1 was only a conclusion.

thoughts.reads: The opium was probably brought from London. The key, having served its purpose, would be hurled away.
thoughts.text: Gregory answers Holmes's points with guesses ('probably', 'would be', 'may be'), not with findings. No chemist, no key and no horse have been found. He has not answered the question of why the horse was taken out at all.

thoughts.reads: He has twice lodged at Tavistock in the summer.
thoughts.text: Simpson has stayed in the district before. That weakens the 'stranger with nowhere to hide a horse' objection, though only a little.

thoughts.reads: The horse may be at the bottom of one of the pits or old mines upon the moor.
thoughts.text: Gregory's fallback: the horse is dead in a mine-shaft. That would explain why it has not been found. But a man who wanted it dead could have done it in the stall, so it does not answer why it was led out.
options: The horse is dead in a pit
The horse is alive and hidden

thoughts.reads: He acknowledges that it is his, and declares that he had lost it.
thoughts.text: Simpson admits the cravat is his and says he lost it.
If he lost it that evening near the stable, someone else could have had it. Its presence in Straker's hand would then not place Simpson at the hollow.
options: Simpson lies, and Straker tore it from him in the fight
It was lost near the stable or on the moor, and Straker or someone else picked it up
Someone used it deliberately to point at Simpson

thoughts.reads: a party of gypsies encamped on Monday night within a mile of the spot where the murder took place. On Tuesday they were gone.
thoughts.text: Gypsies camped within a mile on the night of the murder and had left by Tuesday.

thoughts.reads: might he not have been leading the horse to them when he was overtaken, and may they not have him now?
thoughts.text: Gregory's new theory: Simpson led the horse out to hand it to the gypsies, who have it now. That would explain both why it was taken out and where it went.
options: Gypsies have the horse with Simpson's connivance
Gypsies took it on their own
The gypsies are unconnected

thoughts.text: Their leaving proves little. A camp near a murder, with gypsies the first to be suspected, has every reason to move on. Nothing yet links them to Simpson or to the horse, and the reward argues against their hiding it.

thoughts.reads: It is certainly possible.
thoughts.text: Holmes 'pricked up his ears' at the new element and then answers flatly. The gypsy theory does not seem to engage him.

thoughts.reads: I have also examined every stable and out-house in Tavistock, and for a radius of ten miles.
thoughts.text: Every stable within ten miles has been searched. That counts against 'shut in a building nearby', unless the searchers were looking for a horse that no longer looks like Silver Blaze. The disguise option in t14.3 survives a search of this kind.

thoughts.reads: There is another training-stable quite close, I understand?
thoughts.text: Holmes brings up Mapleton himself, straight after the stable search. A stable two miles off is on his mind.

thoughts.reads: Silas Brown, the trainer, is known to have had large bets upon the event, and he was no friend to poor Straker.
thoughts.text: Silas Brown has large bets on the race and was on bad terms with Straker. He has motive against both the horse and the man.

thoughts.reads: We have, however, examined the stables, and there is nothing to connect him with the affair.
thoughts.text: 'Examined' and found nothing: but the police were looking for Silver Blaze as described, in a yard full of horses. The negative result is only as good as the search.
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must apply the disguise option of t14.3 to Mapleton in particular, rather than accept the police's negative result.

thoughts.reads: And nothing to connect this man Simpson with the interests of the Mapleton stables?
thoughts.text: Holmes checks whether the police's suspect and the rival stable are linked. He is considering more than one hand in the affair, or a different hand altogether.

thoughts.reads: Nothing at all.
thoughts.text: The two motive-holders, Simpson and Brown, are not known to be connected. If both are involved, it is through some link not yet found. If only one is, the other's motive is a coincidence of the betting.

Open at the end of the drive: why the horse was led out rather than harmed in the stall. Whether Simpson drugged anything, now that the paper may have been a ten-pound note. Where the opium was bought, and how a passer-by could count on a dish that hides it. Who opened the locked door, since no duplicate key has been found and Straker had his own. How the cravat reached Straker's hand. Whether the gypsies matter. Whether the searches, Mapleton's included, would recognise the horse if it had been altered. Also still open: Straker's coat and knife, the dog's silence, and the field-glass.

Standing pictures: (a) the police's, Simpson alone or with gypsies, with the horse hidden or dead in a pit; (b) Mapleton, where Silas Brown has the motive and a yard to hide a horse in, though nothing ties him to the night; (c) Straker himself took the horse out, and someone else killed him. None explains everything yet. (a) is the official theory and the weakest on why the horse left the stall.
options: Simpson, with or without gypsies
Mapleton and Silas Brown
Straker's own errand, and an unknown killer

thoughts.reads: by a cluster of houses away to the westward which marked the Mapleton stables
thoughts.text: From Straker's villa, the stable out-building lies across a paddock and Mapleton can be seen on the skyline. The rival stable is in plain view across open moor.

thoughts.reads: his hand was upon a clue, though I could not imagine where he had found it
thoughts.text: Holmes has his clue during the drive, before he has seen any physical evidence. So it comes from facts already told: Holmes's summary or Gregory's talk in the carriage. The reader has the same material and should re-read it.

Which fact set him off? The last topics were the gypsies, the stable searches, Mapleton, and the lack of any link to Simpson. Earlier ones were the curry and the opium, the dog, and the locked door. Nothing yet tells which.
options: Something in Gregory's conversation (gypsies, Mapleton, the searches)
A point from the original facts (curry, opium, dog, door)
The view of the moor and Mapleton itself

thoughts.reads: He has been in your service some years, Colonel Ross?
thoughts.text: Holmes's first questions at the house are about Straker himself: his body and his record of service. He is not asking about Simpson. The victim's character seems to be in question.

thoughts.reads: I have always found him an excellent servant.
thoughts.text: Ross can only vouch for what he saw at work. It is the same testimony as ¶19 and adds nothing about Straker's private life.

thoughts.reads: There was a box of vestas, two inches of tallow candle
thoughts.text: Straker's pockets: matches, a candle stub, pipe and tobacco, watch, five sovereigns, a pencil-case, some papers, and an ivory-handled knife by Weiss & Co., London.

thoughts.reads: two inches of tallow candle
thoughts.text: A candle and matches, on a rainy night walk to a stable where the lad on duty would have a light. Did he expect to need a small light somewhere else, out on the moor? It may only be habit: he also carries a pipe, and the matches would serve that.
options: He meant to need a light out of doors
Ordinary pocket contents of a pipe-smoker

thoughts.reads: It is what we call a cataract knife
thoughts.text: The bloodied knife from Straker's hand is a surgeon's cataract knife.

thoughts.reads: A strange thing for a man to carry with him upon a rough expedition, especially as it would not shut in his pocket
thoughts.text: The 'small knife' is a delicate surgical blade that cannot be folded. It is useless as a weapon and awkward to carry. Why would a trainer own it, and why take it out at one in the morning?

thoughts.reads: It was a poor weapon, but perhaps the best that he could lay his hands on at the moment.
thoughts.text: Gregory's and Mrs Straker's account: uneasy about touts, Straker grabbed the nearest blade from the dressing-table to defend himself.
options: A hasty choice of weapon
He took it for some purpose he had in mind

thoughts.reads: The tip was guarded by a disk of cork which we found beside his body
thoughts.text: A man snatching up a weapon in a hurry does not fit a cork over its tip. And a man in a sudden fight does not stop to take the cork off. The cork lying by the body suggests he had uncovered the blade on purpose, with time to spare. That fits use for a task better than self-defence. The dressing-table detail comes from the wife, who reports what she saw, not why he took it.

Put these together: a blade for a fine cut, a candle for a small light, the coat taken off, and the horse led out to a hollow rather than harmed in its stall. Was Straker meaning to do some delicate cutting to the horse himself, out of sight of the stable? It is only a pattern, and it is far from proved.
options: Straker meant to injure the horse in some subtle way
Straker carried the knife for defence after all
The knife belongs to some other part of his private life
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must join four details spread across the story: the coat, the candle, the cork, and Holmes's question of why the horse was taken out. They must then imagine the trainer as the one who meant to harm the horse, against everything said of his character.

thoughts.reads: a milliner’s account for thirty-seven pounds fifteen made out by Madame Lesurier, of Bond Street, to William Derbyshire
thoughts.text: In Straker's pocket is a Bond Street milliner's bill for £37 15s, made out to a William Derbyshire.

thoughts.reads: Derbyshire was a friend of her husband’s and that occasionally his letters were addressed here
thoughts.text: This is Mrs Straker's explanation, and it is what her husband told her. Letters for a 'friend' coming to Straker's own house, and a bill for that friend in Straker's own pocket, raise the question of whether 'William Derbyshire' is Straker himself.
options: Derbyshire is a real friend
Derbyshire is Straker under another name

thoughts.reads: Twenty-two guineas is rather heavy for a single costume.
thoughts.text: One dress at 22 guineas (£23 2s) makes up most of a £37 bill. That is a huge sum next to a trainer's wages. Straker is described as 'comfortably off' (¶19), yet these clothes belong to a much richer world.

thoughts.reads: However there appears to be nothing more to learn
thoughts.text: Holmes reads the bill closely, item by item, then says there is 'nothing more to learn'. He also says 'Madam Derbyshire', supposing a woman behind the name. The offhand dismissal is itself a signal.

thoughts.reads: Have you got them? Have you found them?
thoughts.text: Mrs Straker's grief and her 'them' (the killers, or the horse as well) reflect the general belief in several attackers. It is no evidence of who they were.

thoughts.reads: Surely I met you in Plymouth at a garden-party some little time ago, Mrs. Straker?
thoughts.text: Holmes has just come down from London. A claimed meeting at a Plymouth garden-party, straight after he studied a dress bill, looks like a feint rather than a real memory.

thoughts.reads: You wore a costume of dove-coloured silk with ostrich-feather trimming.
thoughts.text: He describes an expensive costume, very likely the one on the bill. The question is really: does Mrs Straker own the dresses Straker was paying for?

thoughts.reads: I never had such a dress, sir
thoughts.text: She has never had such a dress. So the costly clothes on the bill in her husband's pocket went to some other woman. This is a test of whether she owns them, not proof of the alias, but the innocent 'friend' story is now harder to keep. Possible reading: Straker, as 'William Derbyshire', was paying for a second woman and needed more money than his wages.
options: The friend is real and Straker only carried the bill
Straker kept a woman under the name Derbyshire
Mrs Straker is lying about the dress

thoughts.text: Working identification: William Derbyshire = John Straker. Holmes's questions seem to point this way, but no handwriting, address or witness has yet confirmed it.
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must link the bill, the 'friend' whose letters come to the house, and Holmes's garden-party feint. They must take the feint as a test rather than a social slip.

thoughts.text: If Straker led a costly double life, he had a reason to want money from the race. He could get it by betting against his own favourite and making sure it lost. That would supply the missing motive for picture (c) in t68.3. The case against Simpson does not require any of this.

Open at the end of the scene: what clue struck Holmes in the carriage. Why Straker carried a cork-guarded cataract knife and a candle, and took the cork off. Whether Derbyshire is Straker and who wears the dresses. If Straker was working against the horse, who killed him and where the horse is now. Still carried over: the cravat in his hand, the curry and the opium, the dog's silence, the locked door, Mapleton, and the field-glass.

Standing pictures after the house: (a) the police's, Simpson alone or with the gypsies. It is now further strained because the knife looks like a tool rather than a weapon. (b) Mapleton and Silas Brown, with the motive but nothing to tie them to the night. (c) Straker, in debt through a second household, took the horse out himself to injure it quietly, and met his death in the hollow. (c) has gained the most in this scene, but it does not yet say who struck the blow.
options: Simpson, with or without gypsies
Mapleton and Silas Brown
Straker's own scheme, with the killer unknown

thoughts.reads: Ah, that quite settles it
thoughts.text: Holmes treats her denial as settling something. That confirms the garden-party remark was a test, and that the dress on Derbyshire's bill was not his wife's.

thoughts.reads: At the brink of it was the furze-bush upon which the coat had been hung.
thoughts.text: The furze-bush with the coat stands right at the rim of the hollow where the body lay.

thoughts.reads: In that case the overcoat was not blown against the furze-bush, but placed there.
thoughts.text: There was no wind, so the coat did not blow there. Someone put it on the bush.

thoughts.reads: Yes, it was laid across the bush.
thoughts.text: 'Laid across' sounds calm and deliberate, not torn off in a fight. The likeliest options in t35.2 are now that Straker took it off himself to have his arms free, or that someone else arranged it. A man in heavy rain who removes his coat at the edge of a hollow meant to do something there. That fits the 'task' reading of the cork-guarded knife.

thoughts.reads: A piece of matting has been laid here at the side, and we have all stood upon that.
thoughts.text: The hollow has been trampled since Monday, but the searchers kept to a mat at the side. Some original marks may survive.

thoughts.reads: one of the boots which Straker wore, one of Fitzroy Simpson’s shoes, and a cast horseshoe of Silver Blaze
thoughts.text: Gregory has brought footwear for comparison: Straker's boot, Simpson's shoe and a shoe of Silver Blaze's.

The prints in the hollow can tell the pictures apart. Simpson's shoe there supports the police theory. Only Straker and the horse would fit Straker's own errand. A set of prints matching none of them would point to a third person.

thoughts.reads: It was a wax vesta half burned
thoughts.text: In the mud of the hollow Holmes finds a half-burned wax vesta.

Straker's pockets held a box of vestas and a candle stub. A match struck in the hollow most likely came from him. So he wanted a light down there, out of sight of the stable on a dark, wet night. That fits the idea of fine work with a small light, the cataract knife and the candle together.
options: Straker struck a light in the hollow for some task
Someone else, such as the killer, struck it
It is an old match, unrelated

thoughts.reads: I only saw it because I was looking for it.
thoughts.text: Holmes expected to find a burnt match. He reasoned to it beforehand, apparently from the candle and vestas in Straker's pockets. So he already believes someone needed a light in the hollow, and the candle was not mere pipe-smoker's habit (t78.2).
Drop the reading of the candle and matches as ordinary pocket contents. Holmes's prediction came true, so a light was used out on the moor.

thoughts.reads: he clambered up to the rim of the hollow, and crawled about among the ferns and bushes
thoughts.text: Holmes says nothing about what the prints showed. He then searches the rim, which is where tracks leaving the hollow would be. He is looking for the way out: most likely the horse's.

thoughts.reads: I have examined the ground very carefully for a hundred yards in each direction.
thoughts.text: The horse was in the hollow, yet Gregory found no tracks leading away within a hundred yards. How did a shod horse leave soft wet ground without a trace?
options: The tracks are there beyond a hundred yards, or the search missed them
The ground near the hollow does not take prints
The horse was led off along some harder path

thoughts.reads: I should not have the impertinence to do it again after what you say.
thoughts.text: Holmes's politeness is ironic. He means to walk the moor himself, and this is the third police search whose negative result he does not take at face value (stables, Mapleton, tracks).

thoughts.reads: I think that I shall put this horseshoe into my pocket for luck
thoughts.text: The horseshoe is not taken 'for luck'. Holmes will try to track Silver Blaze across the moor and match the shoe against hoof-prints. The field-glass may be meant for this open ground.

thoughts.reads: whether we do not owe it to the public to remove our horse’s name from the entries for the Cup
thoughts.text: Ross is thinking of scratching Silver Blaze from Tuesday's race. He is also impatient with Holmes's methods.

thoughts.reads: I should let the name stand.
thoughts.text: Holmes firmly advises keeping the horse entered. He expects Silver Blaze to be alive, found, and fit to run by Tuesday. Gregory's dead-in-a-mine-shaft idea and any 'killed' reading lose ground.

If the horse is alive and close but unfound after searches of every stable for ten miles, the disguise or 'search by description' option of t14.3 looks stronger. Mapleton, in sight across the moor, is the obvious yard where an altered horse could stand among others.
options: Alive and hidden in a stable, perhaps altered
Alive and loose somewhere on the moor
Alive with the gypsies
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must join Holmes's confidence about the race with the failed stable searches and the Mapleton motive, and not just take him to be optimistic.

thoughts.reads: I am very glad to have had your opinion, sir
thoughts.text: Ross's stiff courtesy shows his low opinion of Holmes. It is manner, not evidence.

Open at the end of the scene: what the footprint comparison showed, since Holmes did not say. Who laid the coat on the bush and struck the match, with Straker the likelier. Where the horse went from the hollow without tracks, and where it is if it is alive for Tuesday. What clue struck Holmes in the carriage. Carried over: the cravat in Straker's hand, the curry and the opium, the dog's silence, who opened the locked door, whether Derbyshire is Straker, and Mapleton.

Standing pictures after the hollow. (c) gains again: Straker led the horse to the hollow, took off his coat, lit a match and uncorked a fine blade to do something to the horse unseen, then was struck down. The horse got away alive. (a) Simpson, with or without gypsies, explains neither the laid coat nor the match. (b) Mapleton is now a candidate for where the living horse ended up, more than for who killed Straker. Who struck the fatal blow is still unexplained in every picture.
options: Straker's own scheme; killer unknown; horse alive somewhere such as Mapleton
Simpson, with or without gypsies
Mapleton people as thieves and killers

thoughts.reads: We may leave the question of who killed John Straker for the instant
thoughts.text: Holmes separates the two problems and works on the horse first. He thinks the horse's fate can be settled without knowing who the killer is, so he may believe they are less tightly linked than the police assume (t4.2).

thoughts.reads: The horse is a very gregarious creature.
thoughts.text: A horse that broke loose in the hollow would make for horses: home to King's Pyland or over to Mapleton. It would not run wild, and on the open moor it would have been seen by now.

thoughts.reads: They could not hope to sell such a horse.
thoughts.text: Drop the gypsy theory. They move off whenever there is trouble, they could not sell so famous a horse, and the reward makes theft pointless for them. Their leaving on Tuesday is explained without any guilt.

thoughts.reads: Why should he run wild upon the moor? He would surely have been seen by now.
thoughts.text: The 'bolted and wandering on the moor' branch of the police theory goes too. It already conflicted with t14.2.

thoughts.reads: He is not at King’s Pyland. Therefore he is at Mapleton.
thoughts.text: The argument is only as good as its premise that the horse went off loose to one stable or the other. Holmes calls it a 'working hypothesis'. If the horse is at Mapleton, the police search there (t66.2) failed to recognise him, and that points back to the altered-appearance option of t14.3.

thoughts.reads: This part of the moor, as the Inspector remarked, is very hard and dry.
thoughts.text: This answers t108.1. Near the hollow the ground is hard and takes no prints, so Gregory's empty hundred yards proves nothing. Prints should show again in the wet low ground towards Mapleton.

thoughts.reads: the shoe which he took from his pocket exactly fitted the impression
thoughts.text: Silver Blaze's own shoe matches a fresh track in the wet hollow on the line to Mapleton. The horse left the scene alive, heading that way. The pocketed horseshoe of t109.2 was for exactly this.

thoughts.reads: It is the one quality which Gregory lacks.
thoughts.text: This repeats Holmes's verdict on Gregory (t39.1). The police searched by rule and missed what a guess about the horse's behaviour found. Their other negative results (stables, Mapleton) are also open to doubt.

thoughts.reads: A man’s track was visible beside the horse’s.
thoughts.text: Close to Mapleton a man's footprints join the horse's track.

thoughts.reads: The horse was alone before
thoughts.text: The horse crossed the moor from the hollow on its own. Nobody led it away from the scene of the murder. A man met it only near Mapleton. Whoever was with Straker in the hollow did not take the horse, and that is a blow to the police picture of Simpson leading it off.
Who is the man who caught the horse near Mapleton?
options: Someone from Mapleton, perhaps Silas Brown
Straker's killer, who followed the horse
Simpson

thoughts.reads: The double track turned sharp off and took the direction of King’s Pyland.
thoughts.text: The man first led the horse towards King's Pyland. That looks like an honest finder taking a stray back to its stable.
options: An honest finder returning the horse
A man who set out to return it and then changed his mind

thoughts.reads: saw to my surprise the same tracks coming back again in the opposite direction
thoughts.text: He turned back with the horse. A man who sets out to return a stray and then reverses has changed his mind, most likely because he saw what he could gain by keeping the favourite out of the race.

thoughts.reads: It ended at the paving of asphalt which led up to the gates of the Mapleton stables.
thoughts.text: The track goes in at Mapleton's gates. The horse was taken into the rival stable and kept, not returned. Drop the 'honest finder' reading.

The police 'examined' Mapleton and found nothing, yet the horse went in there. Either it was hidden from the searchers or it stood among the other horses unrecognised. The disguise option of t14.3 now looks strong.
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must hold onto the doubt about searching by description from t64.1 and t66.2, and not assume the horse was moved out again after the police visit.

thoughts.reads: if I were to call at five o’clock to-morrow morning
thoughts.text: Holmes asks a pointed question about who is up at dawn. A stray that reached Mapleton early on Tuesday would be met by whoever was stirring first.

thoughts.reads: he is always the first stirring
thoughts.text: Silas Brown is always the first one up. So he is the likeliest man to have met the loose horse at dawn and led it about. He fits the man's track in t119.1.

thoughts.reads: Be off, or you may find a dog at your heels.
thoughts.text: Brown's bluster and his threat of a dog are manner. They also show how Mapleton keeps strangers away.

thoughts.reads: He started violently and flushed to the temples.
thoughts.text: Holmes whispered a specific charge, most likely an account of the tracks and of Brown taking the horse in. Brown's violent start and his denial ('a lie') show it hit home. His agreeing to talk in private gives more away than the denial does.

thoughts.reads: he cringed along at my companion’s side like a dog with its master
thoughts.text: After twenty minutes Brown is broken and obedient. Holmes's charge was true, and Brown has the horse, or knows where it is, and has given in.

thoughts.reads: It shall be there.
thoughts.text: 'It' is very probably Silver Blaze, and 'there' probably the racecourse on Tuesday. This explains why Holmes told Ross to let the name stand: he expected the horse to be alive and available.

thoughts.reads: Should I change it first or not?
thoughts.text: Brown asks whether to 'change' the horse first. That suggests its appearance has been altered, or can be put back, which is how it stood in the yard unrecognised by the police search.
options: Restore the horse's original appearance
Alter it in some way before handing it over

thoughts.reads: I shall write to you about it.
thoughts.text: Holmes laughs at the question and tells Brown not to change it yet. He is not recovering the horse openly or telling the police. It looks as if he means to stage its return in his own way, perhaps with the slighted Colonel Ross in mind.

thoughts.reads: disregarding the trembling hand which the other held out to him
thoughts.text: Holmes refuses Brown's hand. He holds him in contempt and keeps him under threat ('No tricks'). He is not treating him as Straker's murderer, which fits t120.1: Brown only took in a horse that came to him alone.

Open at the end of the scene: the horse seems settled, alive at Mapleton and perhaps altered. The murder is untouched. Who struck Straker in the hollow, since the horse left alone and nobody led it? The rest is carried over: whether Straker was working against the horse (knife, candle, match, laid coat), whether Derbyshire is Straker, how the cravat got into his hand, who drugged the curry and how a passer-by could rely on it, the dog's silence, the opened door, the clue Holmes had in the carriage, and the field-glass.

Standing pictures. The horse: it got loose from the hollow, wandered towards Mapleton, and Silas Brown took it in at dawn, nearly returned it, then kept and probably disguised it. Brown is a profiteer, not the killer. The gypsies are out. The murder: picture (c) still leads, with Straker leading the horse out to do it some delicate harm and being struck down. The police's Simpson theory has lost the 'led the horse away' step. The killer is unknown in every picture.
options: Straker's own scheme, with an unknown killer
Simpson killed Straker but never had the horse
Someone not yet named

thoughts.reads: A more perfect compound of the bully, coward, and sneak than Master Silas Brown I have seldom met with
thoughts.text: This is Holmes's contempt for Brown. It is a verdict on his character, not new evidence.

thoughts.reads: he perceived a strange horse wandering over the moor
thoughts.text: Holmes's reconstruction, which Brown accepted: Brown was first up at dawn and saw a loose horse on the moor. He recognised Silver Blaze, started to lead him back to King's Pyland, then changed his mind and hid him at Mapleton until after the race.

thoughts.reads: I described to him so exactly what his actions had been upon that morning that he is convinced that I was watching him
thoughts.text: The account is Holmes's inference from the tracks, matched to Brown's square-toed boots. It is not a confession in Brown's own words. Brown's collapse is what confirms it.

thoughts.reads: he perceived a strange horse wandering over the moor
thoughts.text: Brown came on the horse loose and by chance. He did not take it from the hollow and had no part in Straker's death, so far as this account goes. The horse question and the murder question really are separate.

thoughts.reads: from the white forehead which has given the favourite its name
thoughts.text: The white blaze is what identifies the horse. Brown's question 'Should I change it first?' and the failed police search fit together if the blaze has been covered or dyed. Silver Blaze then stood in Mapleton's yard looking like an ordinary horse.

thoughts.reads: an old horse-faker like him has many a dodge
thoughts.text: 'Horse-faker' confirms that the horse was disguised rather than hidden in a cupboard. The police searched by description and missed it, as t66.2 suspected.

thoughts.reads: He knows that his only hope of mercy is to produce it safe.
thoughts.text: Brown's motive has been reversed. Now that he is exposed, harming the horse would ruin him, and producing it safe is his only way out. The horse is in no danger.

thoughts.reads: I am inclined now to have a little amusement at his expense. Say nothing to him about the horse.
thoughts.text: Holmes means to keep the horse's recovery secret and stage its return to surprise the sneering Colonel. That explains 'don't change it yet': the disguise may be part of the joke.

thoughts.reads: this is all quite a minor point compared to the question of who killed John Straker
thoughts.text: Holmes treats the horse as the lesser problem. The murder is still unsolved, and Brown is not the answer to it.

thoughts.reads: we both go back to London by the night train
thoughts.text: Why leave the scene of a murder at once for London? The London leads in the case are the Bond Street milliner, Madame Lesurier, on the Derbyshire bill, and Weiss & Co., the makers of the cataract knife. Holmes apparently thinks the murder will be explained there, through Straker's private life, rather than on the moor.
options: To trace 'William Derbyshire' through the Bond Street milliner
To trace the cataract knife through Weiss & Co.
He thinks the murder needs no more work on the spot

thoughts.reads: I have every hope, however, that your horse will start upon Tuesday
thoughts.text: This is consistent with Mapleton: Holmes knows where the horse is and expects it to run. His 'grave difficulties' about the murderer is said to Ross, and it may not be his real view.

thoughts.reads: Might I ask for a photograph of Mr. John Straker?
thoughts.text: A photograph of Straker to take to London. The obvious use is to show it at the Bond Street milliner and ask whether this is 'William Derbyshire'. It strengthens the working identification Derbyshire = Straker.

thoughts.reads: I have a question which I should like to put to the maid
thoughts.text: What does Holmes want from Edith Baxter? He does not say.
options: Something about the curry: who chose it, or who handled Hunter's portion
Something about Straker's habits, the knife or the dresses
Something about the dog or the stable that night

thoughts.reads: I should prefer to have the horse.
thoughts.text: Ross's scorn is what Holmes plans to play on. It is manner, not evidence.

thoughts.reads: You have a few sheep in the paddock
thoughts.text: A sudden question about sheep, on the way out. Holmes is checking a prediction he had already formed.

thoughts.reads: three of them have gone lame, sir
thoughts.text: Three of the sheep in the King's Pyland paddock have recently gone lame.

thoughts.reads: let me recommend to your attention this singular epidemic among the sheep
thoughts.text: Holmes expected lame sheep. That fits the delicate-cut idea: someone with access to the paddock practised a fine cut on the sheep's legs before trying it on the horse. So the harm meant for Silver Blaze was a subtle laming, a small cut to the leg that makes him run badly and leaves no obvious sign of interference.
options: Someone practised laming on the sheep, and the horse was the real target
The lameness is an ordinary ailment and has nothing to do with the case
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must link the cataract knife, the cork, the candle and match in the hollow and the horse led out, and then see lame sheep as a rehearsal. It also helps to know that a tendon can be nicked to lame a horse.

thoughts.text: This answers Holmes's old question of why the horse was taken out of the stable (t57.1). The cutting needed a light, free arms and privacy, away from the lad and the loft. A slightly lame favourite would lose, and that profits whoever bet against him, Straker included if he was in need of money.

The sheep are in the King's Pyland paddock beside Straker's villa. Practising on them over several days needs someone who belongs there and can come and go unnoticed, not a stranger who arrived on Monday. That points at the household, and above all at Straker.

thoughts.reads: To the curious incident of the dog in the night-time.
thoughts.text: Holmes confirms the absence flagged at ¶34. The stable dog made no noise while the horse was taken out.

thoughts.reads: That was the curious incident
thoughts.text: The dog did not bark, so the man who came at night was someone it knew. Simpson was a stranger whom the dog had been set on that very evening. Put together with the door locked at nine and open at seven, the dog's silence points to a familiar person with a key, most plausibly Straker himself. This answers t33.2: Straker opened the door.

If Straker took the horse out, he needed the duty lad asleep. The opium went into Hunter's portion only, and a curry hides its taste, which a stranger meeting the maid by chance could not have known about. That suggests it was added at the house, by someone who knew the menu. Simpson's paper was then only the ten-pound note.
options: Straker, or someone at the house, put the opium in Hunter's curry
Simpson drugged it at the window after all
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must turn the opium-and-curry problem around, from who had access at the window to who could choose the dish.

thoughts.text: Who struck Straker? Nobody led the horse away (t120.1), and Brown only found it loose afterwards. If Straker was in the hollow cutting at the horse's leg by candle and match, the horse itself could have lashed out. A hoof would serve as the 'heavy weapon' that smashed his skull. His knife would then have cut his own thigh as he fell.
options: The horse kicked him while he was cutting
Simpson, or some other man, came on him in the hollow
An unknown third party
thoughts.hindsight: A first-time reader must give up looking for a human killer and imagine the horse's reaction to being cut. The text has not yet pointed at this.

thoughts.text: Open at the scene's end: who or what struck Straker. How Simpson's cravat got into his hand, perhaps picked up after Simpson lost it. Whether the London trip and the photograph will prove Derbyshire = Straker. What Holmes asked the maid. Who put the opium in the curry. What Holmes saw in the carriage, and why he wanted the field-glass. The horse itself is settled: alive at Mapleton, disguised, and to run on Tuesday.

Leading picture: Straker, living beyond his means as 'Derbyshire', planned to lame his own favourite. He practised on the paddock sheep, had the lad drugged, let himself in past a dog that knew him, and led the horse to the hollow. There he took off his coat, struck a light and uncorked the cataract knife, and died in the attempt, perhaps from the horse's kick. The horse ran loose to Mapleton, where Brown hid and disguised it. Simpson looks like a tout who was in the wrong place. The police theory survives only if Simpson came on Straker in the hollow, and the dog's silence counts against him having been in the stable.
options: Straker's own laming scheme, ended by the horse or an accident
Straker's scheme, ended by Simpson or some other man
The police's Simpson theory

thoughts.reads: bound for Winchester to see the race for the Wessex Cup
thoughts.text: It is race day, the Tuesday. Holmes has kept the recovery secret, so Ross is cold and still believes his horse is lost.

thoughts.reads: I have seen nothing of my horse
thoughts.text: Ross has not seen Silver Blaze. Holmes has not told him that the horse is at Mapleton.

thoughts.reads: I suppose that you would know him when you saw him?
thoughts.text: Holmes knows the horse was disguised at Mapleton and told Brown not to change it back. His question warns that Ross will not recognise his own horse.

thoughts.reads: with his white forehead and his mottled off-foreleg
thoughts.text: Silver Blaze has two identifying marks: the white blaze and a mottled off-foreleg. A faker would have to cover both.

thoughts.reads: You could have got fifteen to one yesterday, but the price has become shorter and shorter, until you can hardly get three to one now
thoughts.text: At 15 to 1 the market rated Silver Blaze at about a one-in-sixteen chance of winning. At 3 to 1 it rates him at about one in four. That is a large move overnight for a horse that has not been seen.

thoughts.reads: Somebody knows something, that is clear.
thoughts.text: Somebody knows the horse will run and is backing him. Only a few people are in on the secret.
options: Silas Brown or Mapleton people, who know the horse will run and are hedging their bets
Holmes himself or his agents
A leak from someone else who has heard the horse is found

thoughts.reads: 4. Colonel Ross’s Silver Blaze (black cap, red jacket)
thoughts.text: Both Silver Blaze and Mapleton's Desborough are on the card.

thoughts.reads: We scratched our other one, and put all hopes on your word
thoughts.text: Ross scratched Bayard and is relying entirely on Holmes's assurance.

thoughts.reads: Five to four against Silver Blaze!
thoughts.text: Silver Blaze is now favourite again. The backing has continued up to the race.

thoughts.reads: a powerful bay horse swept out from the weighing enclosure
thoughts.text: A bay horse comes out in Ross's colours.

thoughts.reads: That beast has not a white hair upon its body.
thoughts.text: The bay with no white hair, running in Ross's colours, is Silver Blaze with his blaze and leg dyed. This is the 'change' Brown offered to undo and Holmes told him to leave.

thoughts.reads: For a few minutes he gazed through my field-glass.
thoughts.text: The field-glass is used on the racecourse, to follow the race at a distance. That is one of the uses guessed at ¶6. It was not, so far as we have seen, a tool of the investigation.

thoughts.reads: passed the post a good six lengths before its rival
thoughts.text: Silver Blaze wins easily, with Desborough second. The horse is plainly unharmed and fit.

thoughts.reads: You have only to wash his face and his leg in spirits of wine
thoughts.text: This confirms the disguise: both the face and the mottled leg were dyed. It also confirms how the police search of Mapleton missed him (t66.2, t124.2).

thoughts.reads: took the liberty of running him just as he was sent over
thoughts.text: 'Don't change it' is now explained. Holmes left the disguise on so that the return would surprise the Colonel who had slighted him.

thoughts.reads: I have done so
thoughts.text: Holmes claims to have the murderer, although he left Dartmoor without arresting anyone. The answer must already be within his reach.

thoughts.reads: In my company at the present moment.
thoughts.text: Who is 'in his company' in the owners' enclosure? Only Watson, the Colonel and the horse are there. A reader who considered t182.3 will expect Holmes to mean the horse.
options: The horse
Colonel Ross
Watson

thoughts.reads: either a very bad joke or an insult
thoughts.text: Ross takes the remark as pointing at himself. A typical reader may briefly wonder too: he was the trainer's master, and he has been cold all along. But nothing in the case links him to the night.
options: Ross is accused
Holmes means someone or something else present

thoughts.reads: I assure you that I have not associated you with the crime, Colonel
thoughts.text: Ross is explicitly cleared. Holmes puts his hand on the horse.

thoughts.reads: The horse!
thoughts.text: Silver Blaze struck the fatal blow, most likely with a hoof. The 'murder' and the 'disappearance' are one event: the horse killed Straker in the hollow and then ran loose.

thoughts.reads: it was done in self-defence
thoughts.text: If the horse acted in self-defence, Straker was attacking it. That fits his laming plan with the cataract knife, by candle and match, with his coat laid aside.

thoughts.reads: John Straker was a man who was entirely unworthy of your confidence
thoughts.text: Holmes confirms that Straker was working against his employer. The Derbyshire double life is not yet stated outright, but it now looks very probable as the motive.
The police theory goes. Simpson killed nobody and never led the horse anywhere. Mapleton only found it afterwards. Simpson was a tout in the wrong place.

thoughts.reads: I shall defer a lengthy explanation until a more fitting time
thoughts.text: Settled: the horse is found and the killer was the horse. Still open, with the explanation deferred: how Simpson's cravat got into Straker's hand. Who put the opium in Hunter's curry, and how the dish was chosen. Whether the London trip with the photograph proved Derbyshire = Straker. What Holmes asked the maid. What struck Holmes in the carriage. Who shortened the odds. Whether the thigh cut came from Straker's own knife as he fell.

Leading picture, now largely confirmed. Straker, untrustworthy and probably funding a second household as Derbyshire, meant to lame his own favourite. He drugged or had drugged the lad, passed the silent dog and led the horse to the hollow. There, by match-light, he uncorked the cataract knife, and the horse kicked him dead. The horse ran towards Mapleton, where Brown hid it under dye. The details of the drugging and the cravat remain for Holmes's explanation.

thoughts.reads: as we listened to our companion’s narrative of the events which had occurred at the Dartmoor training-stables upon the Monday night
thoughts.text: What follows is Holmes's reconstruction, told after the fact. Some of it rests on things found (prints, match, sheep, the milliner). Some of it is inference about a moment nobody saw. Each part should be weighed by what it rests on.

thoughts.reads: the immense significance of the curried mutton occurred to me
thoughts.text: This answers t70.2. The clue that struck Holmes in the carriage was the curry, one of the 'original facts' options and not Gregory's talk. A careful reader had the same material from Holmes's own summary on the train.

thoughts.reads: I went to Devonshire with the conviction that Fitzroy Simpson was the true culprit
thoughts.text: Holmes admits he went down believing Simpson guilty. The reader's early wrong turn (t14.6) was also the detective's.

thoughts.reads: Powdered opium is by no means tasteless.
thoughts.text: This confirms the taste argument of t37.6. A plain dish would have given the opium away and a curry hid it. A passer-by could not have counted on the curry, so the drugger had to be someone who chose the menu.

thoughts.reads: Therefore Simpson becomes eliminated from the case
thoughts.text: Simpson did not drug the curry. Hunter's belief (t36.1) was a mistaken conclusion, and the paper was only the ten-pound bribe (t58.2).

thoughts.reads: Which of them, then, had access to that dish without the maid seeing them?
thoughts.text: Holmes narrows the drugger to Straker or his wife, the only two who could choose curry, and asks which of them could reach Hunter's portion unseen by the maid. He poses the question and, in what follows, never states the answer outright.
options: Straker himself
Mrs Straker, knowingly or not

thoughts.reads: Obviously the midnight visitor was some one whom the dog knew well.
thoughts.text: This confirms t182.1. The dog's silence means the visitor was familiar. Simpson, a stranger the dog had just been set on, is ruled out as the man in the stable.

thoughts.reads: John Straker went down to the stables in the dead of the night and took out Silver Blaze
thoughts.text: This confirms the alternative of t46.4. Straker opened the locked door with his own key and led the horse out. It answers t33.2.

thoughts.reads: For a dishonest one, obviously, or why should he drug his own stable-boy?
thoughts.text: Holmes answers t218.3 only in passing: he takes Straker as the one who drugged the lad. Nothing given clears or implicates Mrs Straker beyond her apparent ignorance of the dress.

thoughts.reads: trainers have made sure of great sums of money by laying against their own horses, through agents
thoughts.text: This supports the motive guessed at t92.3. A trainer bets against his own favourite through agents and then makes sure it loses.

thoughts.reads: it is possible to make a slight nick upon the tendons of a horse’s ham
thoughts.text: The cataract knife was for a subcutaneous nick to the tendon, causing a lameness that would pass for a strain. It was not a weapon, and Gregory's 'best he could lay his hands on' (t82.1) is refuted.

thoughts.reads: It was absolutely necessary to do it in the open air.
thoughts.text: This answers Holmes's own early question (t57.1) of why the horse was taken out. A pricked horse would have woken the lads in the loft.

thoughts.reads: Of course that was why he needed the candle, and struck the match.
thoughts.text: This confirms that the candle and the vesta in the hollow were Straker's light for the operation.

thoughts.reads: men do not carry other people’s bills about in their pockets
thoughts.text: This confirms the reading of the bill as Straker's own, and the garden-party remark as a deliberate test of whether the dress reached his wife (t89.1). 'Derbyshire' is called 'mythical'.

thoughts.reads: Simpson in his flight had dropped his cravat, and Straker had picked it up
thoughts.text: The cravat is explained as lost and picked up, the second option of t60.2. Simpson's denial was true. Holmes offers the purpose ('perhaps' to bind the leg) only as a guess.

thoughts.reads: the steel shoe had struck Straker full on the forehead
thoughts.text: The 'heavy weapon' of ¶35 was the horse's shod hoof, kicking out at the sudden light. This confirms t182.3.

thoughts.reads: and so, as he fell, his knife gashed his thigh
thoughts.text: Watson's self-wound idea is confirmed, though the cause was the fall rather than convulsions. The coat had been laid aside to free his arms for the task, as t97.1 read it.

thoughts.reads: the creature frightened at the sudden glare
thoughts.text: The moment of the kick is pure reconstruction, fitted to the match, the shoe and the wounds. Nobody saw it. It is the only account that fits all the traces, but it is not testimony.

thoughts.reads: What could he practice on?
thoughts.text: This confirms that the lame sheep were Straker's practice. Holmes calls it his 'very long shot': predicted from the practise-first rule, then checked with the lad.

thoughts.reads: who had recognised Straker as an excellent customer of the name of Derbyshire
thoughts.text: This was the London errand of t156.1 and the use of the photograph. The milliner identifies Straker as Derbyshire, so the merge is confirmed by a witness.

thoughts.reads: I have no doubt that this woman had plunged him over head and ears in debt
thoughts.text: The 'dashing wife' is the second household. That the debt drove the plot is Holmes's inference ('I have no doubt'). Straker's bets against the horse are not shown as found, though t220.3 makes them the natural motive.

thoughts.reads: We must have an amnesty in that direction, I think.
thoughts.text: The horse is confirmed as bolting and taken in by Silas Brown, who is left unnamed to Ross and unpunished. This is the price of producing the horse safe (t150.1).

Left unstated at the story's end: exactly how Straker got the opium into Hunter's portion unseen, and what Holmes asked the maid (likely the curry or the handling of the dish). Who shortened the odds before the race. Why Straker took the cravat, which is a guess. The field-glass turned out to be for watching the race only. Mrs Straker is treated, without comment, as having known nothing.

Final picture. Straker, deep in debt as 'Derbyshire', meant to lame his own favourite with a tendon nick after laying against it. He practised on the sheep, chose a curry to hide the opium given to Hunter, and passed the dog, which knew him. He picked up Simpson's lost cravat and led the horse to the hollow. There he struck a light, and the frightened horse kicked him dead; his knife cut his thigh as he fell. The horse ran towards Mapleton, where Brown hid and dyed it. Simpson was only a tout.
